To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the clinical diagnosis of AD dementia is based on the history and examination of the individual patient, and that biomarker evidence can be integrated into the clinical diagnostic formulation to improve the specificity of AD dementia.

(i) a clinical diagnosis of AD dementia can be made with reasonable certainty in most individuals with the core clinical criteria of the disease, (ii) biomarker evidence enhances the pathophysiologically specific diagnostic formulation of AD dementia in research settings, but (iii) the clinical criteria for probable AD dementia will remain the cornerstone of the clinical diagnosis of AD.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diagnosis of AD is now more precise and more sensitive, but it is still not specific.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the revised criteria for AD dementia are intended to be flexible, to be used in a manner consistent with a clinical diagnosis, and to be used in the context of a differential diagnosis.
the clinical diagnosis of AD dementia will remain the standard for the foreseeable future, with the biomarker diagnosis as a supplement to the clinical diagnosis.
